characters.name: Camille
characters.personality: Warm, cheerful, always in a rush

sceneNotes.en: It's morning and you bump into a friendly neighbour on the street who is in a hurry but stops to say hello.

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Works all day until the evening; use "Bonsoir" after dark.

expressions.pronunciationNote: The French r is made at the back of the throat: bon-ZHOOR.

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Polite "vous" form, good for someone you don't know yet.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Link the sounds: "allez-vous" sounds like ah-lay-VOO.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.pronunciationNote: "Bien" is one nasal sound, like "byan" without a clear n.

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Replace "Sam" with your own name.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Say zhuh ma-PELL; the "e" in "je" is very light.

en.contextNote: Polite form for a neighbour you don't know yet.

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: A woman can write "Enchantée"; it sounds the same.

expressions.pronunciationNote: The first sound is a nasal vowel: ahn-shahn-TAY.

en.contextNote: Very common way to end a short chat.
Casual and very common; fine with neighbours once you know them a bit.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Ça va bien, merci. Et vous ?

forms.text: Ça va bien, merci. Et vous ?

en.contextNote: Natural reply that hands the question back.

titles.en: Ordering a Drink at a Café

sceneNotes.en: You sit down on a busy café terrace where a quick, friendly server comes over to take your order.

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Use "madame" for a woman. Adding monsieur or madame is polite with staff.

expressions.pronunciationNote: The "j" in Bonjour is soft, like the s in "measure".

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.

en.contextNote: In France, "un café" means a small, strong espresso.
en.literalGloss: I would-like a coffee, if it you pleases

expressions.pronunciationNote: Voudrais ends in a short "eh" sound, and the final s is silent.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.targetText: Avec du sucre ou sans sucre ?

forms.text: Avec du sucre ou sans sucre ?

en.contextNote: The server asks this quickly, so listen for "avec" and "sans".
en.literalGloss: With some sugar or without sugar?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Sans is a nasal vowel, and you do not pronounce the n.

en.contextNote: To choose the other option, say "Avec du sucre, s’il vous plaît."
en.literalGloss: Without sugar, if it you pleases

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: This is very common in cafés. Add a smile and it is not rude.
en.literalGloss: The addition, if it you pleases

expressions.pronunciationNote: Addition sounds like "ah-dee-SYON".

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.pronunciationNote: Beaucoup sounds like "boh-KOO".

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Je peux avoir un café, s’il vous plaît ?

forms.text: Je peux avoir un café, s’il vous plaît ?

en.meaning: Can I have a coffee, please?
en.contextNote: A common alternative to "Je voudrais". It is slightly more casual.
en.literalGloss: I can have a coffee, if it you pleases?

en.meaning: How much do I owe you?
en.contextNote: Natural when paying at the counter or to the server.

sceneNotes.en: You are at a fruit stall in a French market, asking the vendor about prices per kilo and maybe getting a little surprise.

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Use monsieur for a male vendor. Greeting a vendor first is expected in France.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Bonjour: nasal 'on', soft 'j' like the s in 'measure'.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Les fraises, c’est combien le kilo ?

forms.text: Les fraises, c’est combien le kilo ?

en.meaning: How much are the strawberries per kilo?
en.contextNote: Swap in any fruit: les pommes, les cerises, les abricots.
en.literalGloss: The strawberries, it's how much the kilo?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Fraises: the French 'r' is made at the back of the throat.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.targetText: Six euros le kilo, ma belle !

forms.text: Six euros le kilo, ma belle !

en.meaning: Six euros a kilo, my dear!
en.contextNote: Vendors often use friendly words like ma belle or mon grand. Say it as 'see zeu-RO'.
en.literalGloss: Six euros the kilo, my beautiful

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Softened with 'un peu', which sounds friendly rather than rude.
en.literalGloss: Ah, it is a little expensive

expressions.pronunciationNote: Cher: 'ch' as in 'sh', then an open 'è' sound.

en.contextNote: Bargaining is light at French markets; a polite try is fine.

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Use 'je le prends' for one masculine item, 'je la prends' for feminine.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Prends: nasal 'an', final 's' is silent.

en.meaning: No, thank you, that will be all.
en.contextNote: Better for turning down an extra offer. To decline entirely, say 'Non, merci, pas aujourd’hui.'
en.literalGloss: No, thanks, it will be all

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Ça fait combien, s’il vous plaît ?

forms.text: Ça fait combien, s’il vous plaît ?

en.contextNote: Handy when you point at something or want the total.
More casual and expressive; say it with a smile.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Très bien, je prends un kilo.

forms.text: Très bien, je prends un kilo.

en.contextNote: Useful for saying how much you want to buy.
en.literalGloss: Very well, I take one kilo

sceneNotes.en: You are a visitor looking for the train station, and a passer-by gives you quick directions, so you need to ask them to repeat and slow down.

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Use "madame" for a woman. Say it before you ask your question.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Excusez-moi sounds like "ex-kü-zay mwa".

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Où est la gare, s’il vous plaît ?

forms.text: Où est la gare, s’il vous plaît ?

en.literalGloss: Where is the station, if it pleases you

expressions.pronunciationNote: The French "r" in "gare" is made at the back of the throat.

expressions.speaker: character

en.contextNote: The passer-by says it quickly, so it may sound like one blurred word.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Link the words: "vou-za-lay".

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.targetText: Puis tournez à gauche au feu.

forms.text: Puis tournez à gauche au feu.

en.meaning: Then turn left at the traffic light.
en.contextNote: "À droite" means "to the right".
en.literalGloss: Then turn to left at the light

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Said with rising intonation, this is the normal everyday question form.

expressions.pronunciationNote: "Loin" has a nasal vowel, so do not pronounce a clear "n".

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.targetText: Non, c’est à dix minutes à pied.

forms.text: Non, c’est à dix minutes à pied.

en.meaning: No, it's ten minutes on foot.
en.literalGloss: No, it's at ten minutes on foot

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.pronunciationNote: "Répéter" sounds like "ray-pay-tay".

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Use this when the person speaks too fast for you.
en.literalGloss: More slowly, if it pleases you

expressions.pronunciationNote: "Lentement" has two nasal vowels: "lahn-tuh-mahn".

en.meaning: Thank you very much, have a good day!
en.contextNote: Matches the "Merci beaucoup !" and "bonne journée" formulas from earlier in the chapter.
Feminine form of address, for speaking to a woman.
A natural, friendly alternative that explains why you are asking.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Il y a une gare près d’ici ?

forms.text: Il y a une gare près d’ici ?

en.meaning: Is there a station near here?
en.literalGloss: There is a station near from here?

sceneNotes.en: You bump into a neighbour carrying shopping bags in the stairwell of your new building, and she turns out to be friendly and chatty.

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: A woman would say "nouvelle voisine".

expressions.pronunciationNote: "voisin" sounds like vwah-ZAN, with a nasal ending.

en.contextNote: The neighbour says this warmly and may then invite you for tea later.
Polite and common in everyday speech.
Swap in your own country. Use "du" for masculine countries (du Canada) and "des" for plural ones (des États-Unis).
Rising intonation turns the statement into a question.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.pronunciationNote: The French "r" in "parle" is made at the back of the throat.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Je peux vous aider avec vos sacs ?

forms.text: Je peux vous aider avec vos sacs ?

en.meaning: Can I help you with your bags?
en.contextNote: A natural thing to say when the neighbour is carrying shopping.
en.literalGloss: I can you help with your bags

en.contextNote: Good for answering the tea invitation.
Feminine form for a woman speaking.
Works for any gender.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Vous avez besoin d’un coup de main ?

forms.text: Vous avez besoin d’un coup de main ?

en.contextNote: A more casual, idiomatic way to offer help.
en.literalGloss: you have need of a blow of hand

sceneNotes.en: You hail a taxi to the old town, the traffic is heavy, and the chatty driver quotes a price without using the meter.

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Said at the taxi window or when you get in. Vous is used with a driver.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Libre: the French r is made at the back of the throat.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Dans la vieille ville, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Dans la vieille ville, s’il vous plaît.

en.contextNote: Dans la vieille ville means 'into the old town'. You can also give the name of a street or square.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Vieille sounds like 'vyay', with a y sound at the end.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Vous pouvez mettre le compteur, s’il vous plaît ?

forms.text: Vous pouvez mettre le compteur, s’il vous plaît ?

en.meaning: Can you put the meter on, please?
en.contextNote: Use this when the driver quotes a price without the meter.
en.literalGloss: You can put the meter, please?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Compteur: the p is silent in 'comp-', so it sounds like 'kon-teur'.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Ça va coûter combien, à peu près ?

forms.text: Ça va coûter combien, à peu près ?

en.meaning: About how much will it cost?
en.contextNote: A natural way to ask for the fare before or during the ride.
en.literalGloss: It will cost how much, roughly?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Combien: nasal 'on' then 'byan'.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Vous pouvez vous arrêter ici, s’il vous plaît ?

forms.text: Vous pouvez vous arrêter ici, s’il vous plaît ?

en.literalGloss: You can yourself stop here, please?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Arrêter: the first part sounds like 'a-reh-tay'.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Vous avez la monnaie sur un billet de vingt euros ?

forms.text: Vous avez la monnaie sur un billet de vingt euros ?

en.meaning: Do you have change for a twenty-euro note?
en.contextNote: Avoir la monnaie sur... is the usual way to ask for change on a bill.
en.literalGloss: You have the change on a note of twenty euros?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Monnaie sounds like 'mo-neh'.

en.contextNote: A standard polite goodbye when getting out of the taxi.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Vous pouvez m’emmener dans la vieille ville ?

forms.text: Vous pouvez m’emmener dans la vieille ville ?

en.meaning: Can you take me to the old town?
en.contextNote: Combines hailing the taxi and stating where you want to go.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Avec le compteur, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Avec le compteur, s’il vous plaît.

en.contextNote: A shorter, still polite way to ask for the meter.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Ici, ça ira très bien, merci.

forms.text: Ici, ça ira très bien, merci.

en.contextNote: A relaxed way to say the spot is fine for dropping you off.
en.literalGloss: Here, it will go very well, thanks.

sceneNotes.en: You are at the ice-cream cart outside the school with a child who wants a treat, but only two flavours are left and one scoop is the limit.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.targetText: Je voudrais une glace, s’il te plaît !

forms.text: Je voudrais une glace, s’il te plaît !

en.meaning: I'd like an ice cream, please!
en.contextNote: The child uses tu with the adult.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Glace: the 'a' is open, and the final 'ce' is a soft 's'.

expressions.speaker: learner

en.contextNote: Only two flavours are left.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Chocolat: the final 't' is silent.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Une boule de chocolat, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Une boule de chocolat, s’il vous plaît.

en.contextNote: Said to the ice-cream seller, so it uses vous.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Boule: the 'ou' is like English 'oo'.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.targetText: Je peux avoir une deuxième boule ?

forms.text: Je peux avoir une deuxième boule ?

en.meaning: Can I have a second scoop?
en.contextNote: The twist: the child asks for more.
en.literalGloss: I can have a second ball?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Deuxième: the 'eu' is a rounded 'uh'.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Pas aujourd’hui, une seule boule, d’accord ?

forms.text: Pas aujourd’hui, une seule boule, d’accord ?

en.meaning: Not today, just one scoop, okay?
en.contextNote: Soft and kind. The 'd’accord ?' at the end invites the child to agree.
en.literalGloss: not today, one single scoop, okay?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Aujourd’hui: say it as 'oh-zhoor-dwee'.

en.meaning: Yes, go ahead, eat your ice cream!
en.contextNote: Said once the child has accepted one scoop.
en.literalGloss: yes, go there, eat your ice cream

en.contextNote: 'Elle' refers to the glace, which is feminine.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.pronunciationNote: J’adore: the 'j' sounds like the 's' in 'measure'.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.pronunciationNote: Rien: nasal vowel, 'ryan' without the final 'n' sound.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.targetText: Une boule de vanille, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Une boule de vanille, s’il vous plaît.

en.contextNote: Alternative if the child picks vanilla.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Vanille: the 'ill' sounds like 'ee-y'.

en.contextNote: Feminine form, for a woman speaking. A man writes and says 'désolé' (same sound).

greet_and_introduce: Learner lines use "vous" for a first meeting with a neighbour; "tu" could be fine in some areas or with younger people.
greet_and_introduce: "Sam" is a placeholder name; "Enchanté/Enchantée" agrees with the speaker's gender.
greet_and_introduce: Check that "Et vous, comment vous appelez-vous ?" is not too long for a beginner; "Vous vous appelez comment ?" is a spoken alternative.
cafe_order_drink: Chose "Bonjour, monsieur !" to extend the earlier plain "Bonjour !"; please confirm it feels natural with a server.
cafe_order_drink: In France, "un café" is an espresso, so the "sucre" question fits; for Québec learners "un café" would be a filter coffee.
cafe_order_drink: Check that "Je vous dois combien ?" is not too formal for a terrace.
market_ask_price: Greeting reuses 'Bonjour' plus madame; the vendor is female (Martine), so madame is used. Please confirm natural for a market.
market_ask_price: 'Vous pouvez faire cinq euros ?' is a common light-bargaining phrase; check it sounds natural for a kilo price.
market_ask_price: Free extra (twist) is not in the required slots; 'Non, merci, ce sera tout' works as a polite decline after the vendor adds a gift or offers more.
ask_directions: The scene uses "vous" throughout because it is a stranger-to-stranger situation. Please check that this is right for a young passer-by.
ask_directions: The fast-speech twist is only hinted at in context notes. Please confirm that "Plus doucement ?" is natural for asking someone to slow down, alongside "plus lentement".
ask_directions: Please confirm that "au feu" is natural for "at the traffic light", and whether "aux feux" or "au feu rouge" would be more common.
meet_neighbour: Learner uses "vous" with a neighbour of unknown age, which is the safe default; please confirm.
meet_neighbour: The country in "Je viens d’Espagne" is a placeholder; the preposition changes with the country (d’, du, des).
meet_neighbour: Masculine/feminine "voisin/voisine" is covered by an extra variant; please check that the variant list is enough.
take_taxi: Dans la vieille ville is used for 'to the old town'; please check whether à or dans sounds more natural for a taxi request.
take_taxi: Learner lines use vous throughout since this is a service scene. The greeting, thanks and goodbye reuse earlier formulas (Bonjour, merci, bonne journée).
take_taxi: For Québec, 'la monnaie' and 'compteur' are fine, but 'taxi' could also be 'un taxi' and 'vingt piasses' would be casual slang; none used here.
buy_ice_cream: Learner speaks to the child with tu and to the seller with vous (the scoop line); please confirm the shift feels natural.
buy_ice_cream: Boule is standard in France; in Québec 'une boule' is also common, but 'cornet' and 'crème glacée' are used more often than 'glace'.
buy_ice_cream: 'Je voudrais' for a child is polite; 'Je veux' would also be natural but blunter.
